scenes.title: 1959 Stanford Peg-Board Table: 48 Square Wooden Pegs, '$1 vs $20 Payout Envelopes' & the Inverted '+1.35 vs -0.05' Enjoyment Graph!
scenes.era: 1959, Department of Psychology, Stanford University, California

layout.description: Sunlit high-key 1959 Stanford laboratory room featuring a warm oak table holding the famous **48-Square-Wooden-Peg Board** and **12-Wooden-Spool Tray** alongside an analog stopwatch, two crisp white **Payout Envelopes labeled '$1 Single-Unit Voucher' and '$20 Twenty-Unit Voucher'**, and the inverted private-rating chart showing **$1 Group: +1.35 ('Enjoyable!') vs $20 Group: -0.05 & Control: -0.45 ('Boring!')**.

positions.who: Leon Festinger / J. Merrill Carlsmith (mannequin in 1959 slim tie, short-sleeve white dress shirt, and horn-rim glasses)
positions.where: standing beside the oak peg-board table offering the choice of the '$1 Voucher Envelope' versus the '$20 Voucher Envelope' while pointing to the inverted +1.35 vs -0.05 attitude bars

positions.who: Stanford Undergraduate mannequin (in 1959 collegiate cardigan and chinos)
positions.where: finishing his 60th minute quarter-turning the 48 square wooden pegs with glazed boredom — then leaning forward genuinely smiling (+1.35!) on the private interview scorecard after accepting only the $1 Envelope!

props.name: wooden 8×6 board of 48 square pegs & 12-spool packing tray
props.physical_behavior: makes the absurdity of calling it 'exciting!' immediately comic and clear

props.name: labeled '$1 Single-Unit Payout Envelope' vs '$20 Twenty-Unit Payout Envelope'
props.period_detail: cleanly contrasts tiny insufficient justification against massive external payout

props.name: Private Attitude Rating Chart ('Control: -0.45 | $20 Payout: -0.05 | $1 Payout: +1.35!')
props.period_detail: shows less payout producing dramatically higher genuine liking

actions.verb_sequence: turns square wooden pegs quarter-turn by quarter-turn sighing with boredom -> receives the small '$1 Payout Envelope' and tells a waiting peer the task was fun -> marks **+1.35 Truly Enjoyable** on the private department survey!
contrasts a second student taking the thick '$20 Payout Envelope' who privately marks **-0.05 Boring**

reactions.reaction: nods earnestly having convinced himself the pegs really had a neat rhythm

scenes.wardrobe: 1959 California campus style: crisp white short-sleeve dress shirt with slim dark tie; collegiate knit cardigan, Oxford shirt, chinos.
scenes.lighting: Warm, bright high-key California window daylight.
scenes.recognition_hook: Turn 48 square wooden pegs for one mind-numbing hour: pay students $20 to call it fun and they still hate it — pay them $1 and they convince themselves they loved it!

key_visual.description: a 1959 Stanford lab table with a 48-square-wooden-peg board, labeled $1 and $20 payout envelopes, and a private rating chart where +1.35 ($1) towers above -0.05 ($20)

scenes.title: Waiting-Room Persuasion: Looking a Fellow Student in the Eye

layout.description: Bright wood-paneled waiting room with two chairs outside the peg-board lab.

positions.where: enthusiastically telling the waiting female student confederate 'Honestly, turning those pegs was really intriguing!'

props.name: waiting-room sign-in clipboard
props.period_detail: creates real social accountability to an innocent peer

actions.verb_sequence: leans in pitching the dull task warmly under free choice -> pauses afterward feeling the $1 dissonance pinch

reactions.reaction: resolves tension by upgrading memory of the task

scenes.recognition_hook: Once your own mouth freely tells an innocent classmate 'It's super fun!' for a tiny $1 voucher, your ego rewrites your memory so you aren't a liar!

scenes.title: 1963 Forbidden Toy Test: Why Mild Guidance Beats Giant Threats

layout.description: Sunny playroom rug with five colorful wooden toys including one sleek red fire-truck set aside on a low table.

positions.where: giving either a Mild request vs Severe warning before leaving the child free to rate the toys weeks later

props.name: wooden toy fire-truck & toy preference chart
props.period_detail: children given a MILD reason privately devalued the forbidden toy for weeks; children threatened severely craved it more!

actions.verb_sequence: chooses freely not to play with truck -> weeks later rates other toys higher on own accord

scenes.recognition_hook: Threaten huge punishment and kids obey only while you watch; give mild guidance with choice and they decide for themselves they don't even want it!

scenes.title: Spotting Your Own 'Effort Justification' on Bad Sunk Costs

layout.description: Bright desk where a buyer inspects a tedious subscription / project with a 'Would I Choose This Today at $0?' reality card.

positions.where: catching themselves over-praising an exhausting sunk cost and calmly cutting losses

actions.verb_sequence: compares real enjoyment vs ego defense -> cancels bad commitment cleanly

scenes.recognition_hook: Whenever you catch yourself fiercely praising something that cost you misery for almost zero reward, check whether Festinger's $1 peg-board is talking!
